solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Manifest impatience that I bet wrongly on winner (5,2,3,3)

indicators.note: letters put down wrongly are out of their proper order, so they must be rearranged
in an across clue 'A on B' puts A after B, the way one thing rests on another

annotation.surface: A gambler, having put money on the winner, can't wait for the payout.
annotation.walkthrough: The anagram comes after CHAMP because 'on' in an across clue puts the first-mentioned piece to the right.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a horse champs at the bit, chewing it restlessly, when eager to be off, so people doing it are visibly impatient.

entries.clue: Helpful craftsman, local, scratching head (11)

indicators.note: to scratch something is to strike it out, and the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: NATIVE (a local) without its first letter

annotation.surface: A handy craftsman from the village pauses, puzzled, to scratch his head.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scratching head' reads as a puzzled gesture; here it strikes the N off NATIVE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cooperative person goes along with others and helps, as opposed to being obstructive.

entries.clue: Dread carnage, on and off street (5)

indicators.note: something on and off alternates, so letters are taken on, then off, in turn

annotation.surface: Fear of the bloodshed that flares up now and then on the street.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On and off' looks like it describes the carnage flaring up; it tells you to take every other letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A borrowed German word: angst is a deep, nagging fear, often without a clear cause.

entries.clue: Look with difficulty round a small publisher, in this? (9)

definitions.text: Look with difficulty round a small publisher, in this?

indicators.note: one thing going round another surrounds it, so PEER wraps the other letters

blocks.note: to peer is to strain to see; split PE…ER

annotation.surface: Someone squinting to find a little publishing house through thick weather.
annotation.walkthrough: A pea-souper is a thick yellow London fog, so the whole clue describes one: in it, you would indeed peer to make out a small publisher's office.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: in a pea-souper you can barely see, so you would have to peer hard to find even a nearby office.

entries.clue: More than one fine lady at first clothed in real delicacy (7)

indicators.note: what comes at first in a word is its opening letter
something clothed in a garment sits inside it, so these letters sit inside TRUE

blocks.note: F is fine (on pencils); doubling a letter makes a plural abbreviation, as pp is pages

annotation.surface: Several elegant ladies dressed up in some genuine finery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fine lady' reads as one phrase, a posh woman; the words split, with 'fine' giving F twice and 'lady' only its L.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the truffle is a rare, costly fungus prized by gourmets, one of the classic delicacies.

entries.clue: Carries items on back of camel (5)

blocks.note: to hump is to lug something heavy
a camel has one or two on its back

annotation.surface: A camel carries a load strapped to its back.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface points at luggage piled on the camel; the camel's own humps are the items meant. To hump, meaning to carry with effort, is informal British.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal British humps means lugs something heavy; and a camel's humps are the fatty lumps on its back.

entries.clue: City pub Charlie alone wrecked (9)

indicators.note: something wrecked is smashed up, so the letters of ALONE are broken and reassembled

annotation.surface: Charlie sits drunk and alone in a city bar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wrecked' is slang for drunk, which suits a man alone in a pub.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Barcelona is one city, the Catalan capital on Spain's Mediterranean coast.

entries.clue: One full of alcohol perhaps is expelled from Arab city (3)

indicators.note: someone expelled from a place is thrown out of it, so the letters IS leave TUNIS

blocks.note: the capital of Tunisia, whose last two letters spell IS; those are thrown out

annotation.surface: A drunk is thrown out of a North African city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One full of alcohol' paints a drunkard; it is a tun, a large cask for wine or beer.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a tun is a large cask, and one holding wine or beer is full of alcohol, hence 'perhaps'.

entries.clue: Extensive note put in record (4)

indicators.note: something put in a container goes inside it, so N sits inside LOG

blocks.note: a log is a record, as a ship's log; split LO…G

annotation.surface: A lengthy memo gets filed in the records.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Note' reads as a memo; in wordplay it is just a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something long, like an extensive list, stretches a great way.

entries.clue: A member of corps on dock finally dropped in the shade (10)

indicators.note: what is dropped finally is lost at the end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: a member of the Marine Corps

annotation.surface: A marine on the dockside collapses in the shade.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dropped in the shade' reads as a soldier slumping out of the sun; 'dropped' belongs to the dock, and 'the shade' is a colour.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: aquamarine is one shade, a pale greenish blue named after the gemstone.

entries.clue: Came across entertaining American lounge singer (4,4)

indicators.note: a host entertaining a guest has them in the house, so MET holds A inside it

blocks.note: to come across someone is to meet them; split ME…T
to lounge about is to loaf

annotation.surface: Someone happens upon a crooner entertaining an American in a lounge bar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lounge singer' looks like one phrase for a hotel-bar crooner; 'lounge' is a verb here.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Meat Loaf was one singer, the American rock star behind Bat Out of Hell.

entries.clue: That woman, married, proved old-fashioned (6)

annotation.surface: A woman's marriage showed how traditional she was.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old-fashioned' reads as a verdict on her; it flags an archaic spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: Shewed is an old spelling of showed, and to show a point is to prove it; 'old-fashioned' flags the archaic form.

entries.clue: Saver confused with deceit is gutted (11)

indicators.note: confused things are muddled up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

annotation.surface: A saver tricked by a con is devastated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' is British slang for bitterly disappointed, which fits a swindled saver; here it means disembowelled.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the literal sense: to eviscerate an animal is to gut it, taking out its entrails.

entries.clue: Rewritten document is about politician with feeblest case (10)

indicators.note: one word about another goes round it, so IS surrounds MP
a case holds its contents, so PALEST encloses the rest

blocks.note: pale in the sense of weak, faint; split PAL…EST

annotation.surface: A politician's weak defence is exposed when a document turns out to have been rewritten.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Case' reads as a legal argument; it is a container, and 'feeblest' works through pale in its sense of faint or weak.
annotation.definitionFit: A palimpsest is a manuscript scraped clean and written over, so it is literally a document written a second time.

entries.clue: Naughty lad on cocaine initially had to swear (9)

indicators.note: what happens initially happens at the start, so only the first letter of cocaine is used

blocks.note: to have dinner is to eat it

annotation.surface: A bad boy high on cocaine couldn't help cursing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Had to' reads as 'was obliged to'; 'had' means ate, and 'to' only links to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, formal and rare: to imprecate is to call down curses, which is to swear.

entries.clue: Being late, celebrity cycling round has something to eat (9)

indicators.note: a cycle goes round and back, so the front letter of STAR moves round to the end
one thing round another surrounds it, so TARS wraps DINES

blocks.note: STAR with its S sent to the back; split TAR…S
to dine is to have a meal

annotation.surface: A late-arriving star cycles in and grabs a bite.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' reads as riding a bike; it means rotating letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: tardiness is the noun for lateness, the state of being late.

entries.clue: Leave to be sick, but not very (4)

indicators.note: 'but' means except, so 'but not very' asks for the word without V

blocks.note: to vomit is to be sick
V is very; this letter is removed

annotation.surface: Someone is allowed off work because they are ill, though not seriously.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leave to be sick' reads as sick leave; 'Leave' is the definition on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to leave something out is to omit it.

entries.clue: This blocks sibilant in front of mouth? (4)

definitions.text: This blocks sibilant in front of mouth?

indicators.note: something in something else sits inside it, so S sits inside LIP

blocks.note: the lip is at the front of the mouth; split LI…P
a sibilant is a hissing sound, and S is the letter whose sound it is

annotation.surface: A speech problem where the tongue gets in the way of hissing sounds.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes a lisp: the tongue pushes forward so S comes out as TH.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a lisp is the tongue at the front of the mouth getting in the way of S sounds.

entries.clue: Show of green largely amid crop (10)

indicators.note: something taken largely is taken mostly, so the word loses its last letter
amid means in the middle of, so VERDAN goes inside RICE

annotation.surface: A display of greenery, mostly among the fields of crops.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Green' nods to Ireland, fitting the Irish dance show, as well as meaning verdant.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Riverdance is one show, the Irish step-dancing stage spectacular.

entries.clue: Disappear, having run in for coat (7)

indicators.note: to have something is to hold it, so VANISH holds the letter
'run in' means R goes in, inside VANISH

blocks.note: to vanish is to disappear; split VA…NISH
R for run, as in cricket scores

annotation.surface: Someone vanishes, having dashed inside to fetch a coat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coat' reads as a garment; it is a coat of paint or varnish.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: varnish is one kind of coat, a clear glossy layer brushed onto wood.

entries.clue: Allot gold “star” (6)

blocks.note: to mete out is to allot

annotation.surface: Hand out a gold star.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks show 'star' is used loosely: a meteor is no true star.
annotation.definitionFit: A popular sense flagged by the quotes: a meteor is called a shooting star though it is no star at all.

entries.clue: Minute hands, in relation to face? (5)

definitions.text: Minute hands, in relation to face?

blocks.note: the surface pushes tiny hands, 'minute' as in small; the setter means the minute hand of a clock, and the hour hand beside it
the surface suggests hands compared in size with a face; the setter means relative to a round clock face, where each hand reaches from the centre towards the rim

annotation.surface: Tiny hands, compared with the size of the face.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Minute' reads as tiny (my-NOOT); it is the minute hand, which, like the hour hand, is a radius of the clock face.
annotation.definitionFit: Clock hands run from the centre of the round face towards its edge, so in geometric terms they are radii.

entries.clue: Not so good to contribute to a little light teasing (8)

indicators.note: what contributes to something goes into it, so ILLER is put into RAY

blocks.note: a ray is a thin beam of light; split RA…Y

annotation.surface: Some light teasing that isn't very kind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A little light teasing' reads as one gentle phrase; 'teasing' stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: raillery is good-humoured banter at someone's expense.

entries.clue: Scales not fully calibrated (5)

indicators.note: a word used not fully is only partly there, so the answer is a piece of it

annotation.surface: A set of weighing scales that has not been properly calibrated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scales' reads as weighing scales; it is the zodiac sign whose symbol is a pair of scales.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossword favourite: Libra is the constellation and star sign whose name and symbol are the scales.

entries.clue: Return of service plus extra run covering great area (3,3,4)

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so RAF is read backwards

blocks.note: RAF, the Royal Air Force, a military service, turned round
in cricket, a wide is an extra run given when the ball is bowled out of the batsman's reach

annotation.surface: A tennis return, plus an extra run to cover lots of court.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Return of service' looks like tennis; 'service' is the armed forces.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: something spread far and wide reaches in every direction, covering a great area.

entries.clue: Answer the same as before? Bother! (3)

annotation.surface: An exasperated person gets the same answer as last time.
annotation.walkthrough: DO is short for ditto, the mark meaning the same as above.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: ado is fuss and trouble, as in 'without further ado'.

entries.clue: Stick by hot tub (4)

blocks.note: a bat is a stick for hitting a ball

annotation.surface: Stay close to the hot tub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stick by' reads as stay loyal to; 'Stick' is a noun here.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a tub, in everyday speech, is the bath you wash in.

entries.clue: Donning hat, set out for Brief Encounter (3-5,5)

indicators.note: letters set out are laid out afresh, so they are rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone puts on a hat and sets off to see the film Brief Encounter.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals make it look like the 1945 film about a doomed railway-station romance; read plainly, it is a short fling.
annotation.definitionFit: A cheeky reading of the film title: a one-night stand is a romantic encounter that is over by morning.
